title: Question 2
stem:
A spacecraft in deep space uses jets of hot gas from its thrusters to change its velocity. Fig. 2.1 shows a side view of the spacecraft and some of its thrusters.

{{figure:figure_2_1}}

Fig. 2.1 (not to scale)

Thruster A is a distance of $1.6\text{ m}$ leftwards from the centre of gravity of the spacecraft. Thruster C is a distance of $0.40\text{ m}$ upwards from the centre of gravity of the spacecraft.

Thrusters A and B can produce forces on the spacecraft in the upwards direction only. Thruster C can produce a force on the spacecraft in the leftwards direction only. All the thrusters shown produce forces entirely in the same plane as the centre of gravity.

parts.label: (a)(i)
parts.text:
Thruster A is activated, producing a force of $60\text{ N}$ upwards on the spacecraft. Thruster C is also activated, producing a force of $220\text{ N}$ in the leftwards direction on the spacecraft.

Calculate the resultant moment due to these forces about the centre of gravity.
hints: Hint 1: Look at each thruster separately and pick out the perpendicular distance from its line of action to the centre of gravity from Fig. 2.1.
Hint 2: Work out each moment with $F \times d$ and think about whether they try to turn the spacecraft the same way or opposite ways before subtracting.
parts.proper_answer: Moment due to A $= 60 \times 1.6 = 96\text{ N m}$, moment due to C $= 220 \times 0.40 = 88\text{ N m}$ in opposite sense. Resultant moment $= 96 - 88 = 8.0\text{ N m}$ about the centre of gravity.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Recall what a moment needs**
Think moment as turning effect about a point. You need the size of the force and the perpendicular distance from the centre of gravity to the line of the force, so $$\text{moment} = F \times d.$$

Step 2: **Calculate the two moments and combine**
For thruster A: $$M_A = 60 \times 1.6 = 96\text{ N m}.$$ For thruster C: $$M_C = 220 \times 0.40 = 88\text{ N m}.$$ They act in opposite rotational senses, one clockwise and one anticlockwise, so subtract: $$M_{resultant} = 96 - 88 = 8.0\text{ N m}.$$

resultant moment as sum with direction

parts.label: (a)(ii)
parts.text: State and explain whether the forces from A and C are a couple.

markscheme_points.text: the resultant force (of A and C) is not zero or forces (from A and C) are not parallel or forces (from A and C) are not equal (magnitude) or forces (from A and C) are not opposite (direction) or forces (from A and C) act through the same point so (they are) not a couple

hints: Hint 1: Recall the two strict tests for a couple - what must be true about the size, direction and lines of the two forces for resultant force to be zero with only turning?
parts.proper_answer: Not a couple because the resultant force is not zero. The two forces are not equal in magnitude, not parallel and not opposite in direction.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Test against the definition of a couple**
A couple is two forces that are equal in size, opposite in direction and parallel, but separated. Their vector sum is zero so there is pure turning with no resultant force. Here A acts upwards with $60\text{ N}$ and C acts leftwards with $220\text{ N}$. They are perpendicular, different sizes and do not cancel, so the resultant force is not zero and they cannot be a couple.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text:
Thrusters A and C are now switched off and the spacecraft is stationary. Thruster B is activated at time $t_{1}$, producing a constant force on the spacecraft until the fuel runs out at time $t_{2}$. As the fuel is used, the total mass of the spacecraft decreases.

On Fig. 2.2, sketch the variation of speed of the spacecraft with time from $t_{1}$ to $t_{2}$.

{{figure:figure_2_2}}

Fig. 2.2

markscheme_points.text: line with a positive gradient from (t1, 0) to t2
line with increasing positive gradient from t1 to t2

hints: Hint 1: Start from $F = ma$ with constant $F$ but falling $m$ and ask yourself what must happen to $a$, and what $a$ means on a speed-time graph.
Hint 2: Remember the spacecraft starts stationary at $t_1$, so decide the starting point and whether the slope should stay constant or get steeper as mass is lost.
parts.proper_answer: Curve starting at (t1, 0) with positive gradient, with gradient increasing with time up to t2.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Link force, mass and acceleration**
Thruster B gives a constant force $F$. From $$F = ma$$ then $$a = \frac{F}{m}.$$ As fuel is used $m$ decreases, so $a$ must increase even though $F$ is constant.

Step 2: **Translate to speed-time shape**
On a speed-time graph the gradient is acceleration. Speed starts at zero at $t_1$. Because speed is increasing, the gradient is positive. Because acceleration is increasing, the gradient gets steeper with time. So draw a curve from $(t_1,0)$ that bends upwards to $t_2$.

parts.label: (c)(i)
parts.part_stem:
The spacecraft now splits apart into a carrier and a payload as shown in Fig. 2.3.

{{figure:figure_2_3}}

Fig. 2.3

During the split, an average force of $5500\text{ N}$ acts on the payload for a time of $0.36\text{ s}$. The velocity of the payload increases by $8.5\text{ m s}^{-1}$ in the upwards direction.

The combined mass of the carrier and payload is $2.5 \times 10^{3}\text{ kg}$.
parts.text: State the principle of conservation of momentum.

markscheme_points.text: sum / total momentum before = sum / total momentum after or sum / total momentum (of a system of objects) is constant
if no (resultant) external force / for an isolated system

hints: Hint 1: Think about what quantity stays the same when objects push on each other - focus on total momentum before compared with total after.
Hint 2: Remember this is only true under a special condition about outside influences - when would outside forces spoil the conservation?
parts.proper_answer: The total momentum of a system remains constant provided no resultant external force acts on the system.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **State the conserved quantity**
In any collision, explosion or split, it is the vector sum of all the momenta that matters. The principle says total momentum before the event equals total momentum after.

Step 2: **Add the condition**
This only holds if the system is isolated, meaning no resultant external force acts. Internal forces between carrier and payload cancel in pairs, but an outside push would change the total.

parts.label: (c)(ii)
parts.text: Show that the mass of the payload is $230\text{ kg}$.
hints: Hint 1: Link the given average force, time and velocity change - which law connects force to rate of change of momentum?
Hint 2: Rearrange to make mass the subject before putting in $5500\text{ N}$, $0.36\text{ s}$ and $8.5\text{ m s}^{-1}$, and check the value rounds to $230\text{ kg}$.
parts.proper_answer: Using $F\Delta t = m\Delta v$, $m = F\Delta t / \Delta v = 5500 \times 0.36 / 8.5 = 233 \approx 230\text{ kg}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Use impulse equals momentum change**
The push gives the payload extra momentum. Impulse is force times time and equals change in momentum: $$F\Delta t = \Delta p = m\Delta v.$$

Step 2: **Rearrange and substitute**
Make $m$ the subject: $$m = \frac{F\Delta t}{\Delta v}.$$ Then $$m = \frac{5500 \times 0.36}{8.5} \approx 2.3 \times 10^2\text{ kg}.$$ This shows the mass is $230\text{ kg}$ to two significant figures. Equivalently $F = ma$ with $a = \Delta v / \Delta t$ gives the same result.

parts.label: (c)(iii)
parts.text: Calculate the magnitude of the change in velocity of the carrier.

markscheme_points.text: Δv = 0.87 m s⁻¹ or 0.86 m s⁻¹
Δv = 0.87 m s⁻¹ or 0.86 m s⁻¹

hints: Hint 1: First find the momentum gained by the payload in the split using either $F\Delta t$ or $m\Delta v$.
Hint 2: Think about what mass is recoiling the other way - how do you get the carrier mass from the combined $2.5 \times 10^3\text{ kg}$?
Hint 3: Equate the magnitudes of momentum change for carrier and payload and rearrange to find the carrier velocity change.
parts.proper_answer: Change in momentum $\approx 5500 \times 0.36 = 1980\text{ N s}$. Carrier mass $= 2.5 \times 10^3 - 230 = 2270\text{ kg}$. Change in velocity $= 1980/2270 \approx 0.87\text{ m s}^{-1}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Find the momentum transferred**
The impulse on the payload is: $$\Delta p = F\Delta t = 5500 \times 0.36 = 1980\text{ N s}.$$ This is also $m\Delta v = 230 \times 8.5$. By Newton's third law the carrier gets an equal opposite impulse.

Step 2: **Get the carrier mass**
The carrier is what is left after the payload separates: $$m_{carrier} = 2.5 \times 10^3 - 230 = 2270\text{ kg}.$$

Step 3: **Find the carrier velocity change**
Set the carrier momentum change equal to the impulse magnitude: $$m_{carrier}\Delta v_{carrier} = \Delta p.$$ So $$\Delta v_{carrier} = \frac{1980}{2270} \approx 0.87\text{ m s}^{-1}.$$
